terminal.description: A shell in your workspace: node run.mjs <file> runs the query in that file against a fresh copy of Mallowfield's database and prints the rows.

tasks.title: List the customers the round-up leaves out
tasks.description:
Show Dunstan who is missing from his round-up.

In `queries/1-left-out.sql`, return two columns, in this order:

- `id`
- `customer`: the customer's name

One row for every customer with no order placed on or after `2026-01-01`, those who never ordered at all included. Any order of rows. Check compares the columns and the rows on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Run `2-round-up.sql` and compare its names with `customers` in `seed.sql`.
Pair each customer with their orders from 2026 only, keeping every customer.
Keep the customers who found no partner.
hints: A customer with only old orders is as missing as one with none. Read the lesson's part "See it for yourself".
Put the date test in the `ON` of a `LEFT JOIN` to orders, then keep the rows where the order's id is `NULL`. If you use `NOT IN` instead, remember the empty win-back list.
The query has the shape `SELECT c.id, c.name AS customer FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.placed_at >= '2026-01-01' WHERE o.id IS NULL`.

tasks.title: Give every customer a line on the round-up
tasks.description:
Fix the round-up in `queries/2-round-up.sql` at the cause.

It returns one row for every customer, with two columns, in this order:

- `customer`: the customer's name
- `spent_pence`: what their orders placed on or after `2026-01-01` came to, `0` when none

Any order of rows. Check compares the rows on the data you can see and on hidden data, where customers have other mixes of old and new orders.
nextSteps: Run the file and count the rows. Find Agata Kowalczyk in `seed.sql` and look at her orders.
Say what the `WHERE` does to a customer the `LEFT JOIN` kept with no partner, and to one whose orders are all old.
Move the date test to where it chooses partners, and run the file again.
hints: Read the lesson's part "How it happens". The `LEFT JOIN` keeps Agata; something after it removes her.

A test in `WHERE` runs on the joined rows and throws away whole customers. A test in the `ON` of the join to orders only decides which orders count as partners. Adding `OR o.placed_at IS NULL` mends only the customers with no orders at all.
The join to orders has the shape `LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.placed_at >= '2026-01-01'`, and the query has no `WHERE`.

videos.title: Why a LEFT JOIN can act like a plain JOIN

tasks.title: Put every seed on the re-order list
tasks.description:
Dunstan orders seed from the growers with the list in `queries/3-november-packets.sql`. Nobody has complained yet.

Fix it so it returns one row for every seed, with two columns, in this order:

- `product`: the seed's name
- `packets`: how many packets of it were in orders placed in November 2026, `0` when none

Any order of rows. Check compares the rows on the data you can see and on hidden data, which has seeds sold only in October and a seed never sold.
nextSteps: Run the file and count the seeds. Which are missing?
Try moving the test on the date into the `ON` of orders. Run it and look at Scarlet runner bean: are October's packets still counted?
Make the test decide which lines reach the seed, not only which orders.
hints: The test is on orders, but the packets are on the lines. Read the lesson's part "When the test is two tables away".

A line whose order is not from November still pairs with its seed, so moving the test into the `ON` of orders still adds its packets. Total November's packets per seed in a query in brackets, then join that to every seed.

The FROM part has the shape `FROM products AS p LEFT JOIN (SELECT l.product_id, SUM(l.packets) AS packets FROM order_lines AS l JOIN orders AS o ON o.id = l.order_id WHERE o.placed_at LIKE '2026-11%' GROUP BY l.product_id) AS n ON n.product_id = p.id`, with `COALESCE(n.packets, 0)`.
